title: Access Control Models
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 5: Identity and Access Management (IAM): Access Control Models.

items: Data owner decides who gets access
Based on Access Control Lists (ACLs)
Most flexible but least secure model
Subject identity determines access (identity-based)
Used in most commercial operating systems (Windows NTFS, Linux permissions)

blocks.text: From Stewart: "The DAC model allows the owner of data to modify permissions on the data. In the DAC model, objects have owners, and the owners can grant or deny access to objects that they own." From Chapple: "Identity-based access control is a subset of DAC because systems identify users based on their identity and assign resource ownership to identities." DAC Weakness: Users can share or delegate access without centralized control. A user who owns a file can grant access to anyone, potentially violating organizational security policies. ⚠️ Exam Trap: DAC is the LEAST restrictive model. The owner has full control. This is the default in most operating systems.

items: System enforces access based on security labels and clearances
Users cannot change access permissions (only administrators)
Uses classification labels (Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, Unclassified)
Most restrictive model; used in government/military
Based on Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality) and Biba (integrity) models

blocks.text: From Shon Harris: "MAC Operating systems enforce the system's security policy through the use of security labels." From Stewart: "The MAC model uses labels to assign access based on a user's need to know and organization policies." From Chapple: "When documented in a table, the MAC model sometimes resembles a lattice." MAC requires:

items: Every subject has a security clearance
Every object has a classification label
System compares clearance to label for every access request
Administrators (not users) manage labels and clearances

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: MAC is SYSTEM-ENFORCED. Even the data owner cannot override MAC restrictions. DAC is OWNER-CONTROLLED. Know this fundamental distinction.

items: Access based on job role/function, not individual identity
Users assigned to roles; roles assigned permissions
Simplifies administration in large organizations
Supports separation of duties and least privilege
Most commonly used model in enterprise environments

blocks.text: From Shon Harris: "RBAC Access decisions are based on each subject's role and/or functional position." From Stewart: When organizations need new capabilities, "they would define the privileges needed for these new roles and how they plan on assigning the privileges, such as with groups." RBAC Components:

items: Users — Assigned to roles
Roles — Collections of permissions
Permissions — Access rights to resources
Sessions — Active user-role associations
Simplified administration (manage roles, not individual users)
Easy to enforce least privilege and SoD
Supports compliance requirements
Reduces administrative errors
Access based on attributes of subject, object, environment, and action
Most flexible and granular model
Uses policies that evaluate attributes at access time
Attributes: user role, department, time of day, location, resource sensitivity
Ideal for cloud and complex environments

blocks.text: ABAC Policy Example: "Allow access to financial reports IF user.role = 'Finance' AND user.clearance >= document.classification AND time = business_hours AND location = 'corporate_network'" ABAC vs RBAC:

items: Access decisions based on predefined rules (IF-THEN)
Rules applied uniformly to all users (not individual-based)
Firewalls are the classic example (ACL rules)
Can be combined with other models for layered control
Rules typically managed by administrators, not users

blocks.text: From Stewart: "A rule-based access control model uses rules to determine access." From the Official CBK: Rule-based access control "reviews an incoming packet to determine if it comes from an IP address that is allowed, while a file-system reviews the current user against the file's ACL to determine if the requested action is allowed." ⚠️ Exam Trap: Rule-based is NOT the same as role-based. Rule-based uses predefined rules (like firewall ACLs). Role-based uses job function/role assignments. The names sound similar but function differently.

items: Access decisions factor in real-time risk assessment
Considers context: location, device, behavior, time
May require additional authentication for high-risk access
Supports adaptive authentication (step-up when risk is detected)
Used by modern zero trust implementations
